title: Send button is enabled while the send handler silently discards the message
description:
**Reported by a separate analysis session 2026-09-16; CONFIRMED in code by me the same day.**

`handleSendMessage` (`EnabledWorkspace.tsx:358`) returns silently:

    if (!selectedItem || !selectedChannelId || !addressedBotId || composerSendBlocked) return;

## The precise mechanism, which the original report did not name

`addressedBotId` is `useState<string>("")` — it starts **falsy** (`EnabledWorkspace.tsx:113`).

The send button's disabled state is `isSendDisabled={composerSendBlocked}`, and `isComposerSendBlocked(sending, turn)` is only:

    return sending || turn !== null;

`addressedBotId` is **not** part of it.

So the guard rejects on a condition the disabled state does not cover. The button is **enabled**, fully clickable, and does nothing. That is the defect: the predicate that decides whether sending is possible and the predicate that decides whether the control looks possible disagree. Either one alone would be fine.

The same applies to Enter in the composer, which routes to the same handler.

## Why it matters beyond the annoyance

A person's first impression of a channel with no bot yet, or during the window before the bot selection resolves, is a send button that swallows their message with no explanation. There is nothing to read, nothing to retry, and no reason to believe the product works.

## Suggested fix

Make the two predicates one. If sending is impossible, the control must show it, and the reason must be legible — "no bot in this channel" is a different message from "waiting for the current turn." Do not solve this by only adding an error banner after the click; the control should not invite a click it will discard.

## Done when

There is no state where the send control is enabled and pressing it does nothing. Each blocked reason surfaces its own message. A test covers the empty-`addressedBotId` case specifically, since that is the state a channel starts in.
